old_text: The tax incentives, while important, were actually less radical than often portrayed. The zone offered a 10% corporate tax rate on export profits when Ireland's standard rate ranged from 40% to 50%. This competitive but sustainable rate would later inspire Ireland's nationwide 12.5% corporate tax rate. The low rate and assurance against sudden changes allowed companies to make long-term investment decisions.
new_text: Shannon's early incentives included exemption from tax on qualifying trading profits. A later regime, effective from 1 January 1981, applied an effective corporation-tax rate of up to 10% to manufacturing profits across Ireland; the Finance Act 1981 extended it to qualifying non-manufacturing activities at Shannon. Companies protected by earlier relief could continue claiming it until 5 April 1990. Ireland's general 12.5% rate on trading income took effect in 2003. Dáil Committee on Public Expenditure, 29 April 1986, §3.12. Revenue, Annual Report 1985, p. 179. Revenue, May 2015, p. 1.

old_text: Operational success within a zone did not make its institutional knowledge portable. A company expanding from Shannon to Singapore gained no advantage from the record it had built at home. Shannon's knowledge of its track record, compliance history, and creditworthiness stayed within its jurisdiction. The company had to establish itself anew.
new_text: Operational success within a zone did not make all of its institutional records usable elsewhere. A company expanding from Shannon to Singapore could bring its commercial history, but the receiving authorities still needed evidence that met their own registration, licensing, and compliance requirements. Recognition agreements could reduce some of that repeated work.

old_text: Shannon also demonstrated the limitations of the traditional zone model. Despite its success, Shannon remained relatively small—never exceeding 10,000 jobs—and its benefits remained largely local to the mid-west region. The zone couldn't easily share its innovations with other regions or countries. Each new zone had to learn the same lessons, make the same mistakes, and build the same infrastructure from scratch. This inefficiency is precisely what our network model addresses.
new_text: Shannon also raises a question about the reach of a successful zone. Local services and institutional knowledge may benefit businesses nearby without becoming readily usable in another legal system. The network proposal addresses the work required to transfer that knowledge and recognize the records it produces.

prefix: Consider a company that spent five years
old_text: Consider a company that spent five years building a compliance record in Singapore's regulatory ecosystem. When expanding to Dubai or London, that entire track record became worthless. The company had to start over, rebuilding relationships, demonstrating reliability, and establishing credibility from scratch. This inefficiency multiplied across thousands of companies and dozens of jurisdictions, creating enormous friction in global commerce.
new_text: Consider a company that has spent five years building a compliance record in Singapore. When it expands to Dubai or London, that history may help it demonstrate reliability, but it does not itself supply the permissions required there. Translation, certification, updated checks, and local approvals can still make expansion expensive.

old_text: The EDB's operations in the 1960s resembled a startup more than a government agency. Young officers, many just returned from overseas education, were given extraordinary authority and resources. They actively recruited investors. EDB offices were established in New York, London, Tokyo, and Zurich, staffed not by traditional diplomats but by deal-makers with the authority to negotiate on the spot. When Texas Instruments executives visited Singapore in 1968, they expected the usual developing country experience: multiple agencies, unclear authority, endless delays. Instead, they found EDB officers who could approve incentives immediately, arrange land within days, and guarantee infrastructure within months.
new_text: The EDB actively recruited investors and coordinated the services needed to establish operations. Its ability to connect investment promotion with industrial planning gave companies an identifiable counterpart. For a new zone, the relevant lesson is that an investment offer needs an institution capable of arranging the land, infrastructure, skills, and approvals on which the offer depends.

prefix: But the research side proved more challenging
old_text: But the research side proved more challenging. Despite massive investments and recruited talent, breakthrough innovations remained elusive. Many star scientists left after their contracts ended. The research institutes produced papers but not patents. The biotech startups that emerged struggled to compete globally. Singapore learned that innovation ecosystems couldn't be engineered like industrial estates. They required cultural changes that went deeper than policy.
new_text: Research capacity and commercial innovation require separate measures. Laboratories, publications, patents, clinical results, and viable businesses represent different outcomes. In 2009, Singapore's Ministry of Health described the second phase of its biomedical initiative as building translational and clinical research alongside basic science. The question for zone policy is how research connects to practical uses, and over what period those uses should be assessed. Singapore Ministry of Health, 2009 biomedical sciences announcement.

old_text: The digital economy push from 2014 showed that Singapore had learned from the biomedical experience. Instead of trying to create innovation from scratch, Singapore focused on becoming the best place to deploy innovation. The Smart Nation initiative didn't aim to make Singapore a technology creator but a technology adopter. Every government service would be digitized. Every building would be smart. Every transaction would be electronic. Singapore would be the world's testbed for urban technology.
new_text: The Smart Nation initiative, launched in 2014, linked technology adoption with opportunities for innovation. Its initial platform plan included sharing protected sensor data, improving public services, and enabling businesses to create new services. It treated the city as a place to test and apply technology, with public infrastructure supporting private development. IDA, Smart Nation Platform factsheet, June 2014, p. 3.

prefix: This strategy played to Singapore's strengths
old_text: This strategy played to Singapore's strengths while acknowledging its limitations. Singapore might not create the next Google, but it could be Google's Asian headquarters. It might not invent autonomous vehicles, but it could be the first country to deploy them commercially. It might not pioneer blockchain, but it could have the most comprehensive regulatory framework for digital assets. Innovation through adoption rather than invention became the new model.
new_text: This approach gives a zone two related tasks: attract firms that develop technology and provide conditions in which useful technology can be adopted. The balance depends on local skills, customers, research institutions, and regulatory requirements. Adoption can create opportunities for local improvement without guaranteeing that a global technology company will emerge.

prefix: The recovery strategy revealed Singapore's adaptability
old_text: The recovery strategy revealed Singapore's adaptability. Instead of trying to return to the pre-pandemic normal, Singapore accelerated changes that COVID had initiated. Digital payments became mandatory in markets. Remote work became permanent for suitable jobs. Travel bubbles replaced open borders. Vaccine differentiation replaced lockdowns. Singapore adapted its model rather than defending it.
new_text: The pandemic made digital services, remote work, border controls, and public-health conditions part of business continuity planning. For a connected zone, these are operating dependencies to review as circumstances change. An arrangement that works during normal travel may need a different procedure when people cannot cross a border.

prefix: The early days of the Shenzhen SEZ
old_text: The early days of the Shenzhen SEZ were chaotic beyond contemporary comprehension. The first regulation was just seven pages long, essentially saying "foreign investment is allowed" without specifying how. The first joint venture contract was handwritten because no one had a typewriter. The first factory was built in a converted warehouse because there were no industrial facilities. The first foreign bank operated from a hotel room because there were no office buildings. Everything was improvisation.
new_text: Shenzhen's early development required new administrative procedures as well as physical construction. Opening a market involved decisions about investment, employment, land use, and finance. The following examples show why a zone's rules and institutions must develop alongside its factories.

old_text: The first land auction in 1987 was even more consequential. In socialist doctrine, land belonged to the people collectively and couldn't be sold. Shenzhen found a workaround: land use rights could be transferred for specified periods. The auction was conducted in secret, with bidders unsure if they were participating in reform or crime. When the hammer fell, China had created a land market that would eventually generate trillions in revenue for local governments and fuel the greatest construction boom in history.
new_text: Shenzhen's 1987 land-use-rights auction illustrated the distinction between ownership of land and rights to use it. Land could remain publicly owned while a transferable, time-limited right supported development. The broader lesson is that a new market requires legally defined rights and a procedure for transferring them.

prefix: The environmental catastrophe that accompanied China's rise
old_text: The environmental catastrophe that accompanied China's rise serves as a warning to all developing countries. The health costs, ecosystem destruction, and climate impact of China's development model likely outweigh much of its economic gains. Modern zones must be sustainable by design, not by retrofit. The technology now exists to develop cleanly from the start—there's no excuse for repetition of China's mistakes.
new_text: The environmental damage associated with rapid industrialization is part of its development cost. Aggregate growth cannot show whether particular communities, workers, or ecosystems benefited. A modern zone needs to measure pollution, resource use, and health effects alongside production, and assign responsibility for prevention and remediation.

old_text: Perhaps most importantly, China's experience shows that context matters enormously. China's size, state capacity, cultural homogeneity, and historical moment created conditions that can't be replicated. Other countries that tried to copy China's model—Ethiopia most notably—failed because they lacked China's unique characteristics. Modern zones need to adapt these lessons to local conditions.
new_text: China's experience also shows why context matters. Market size, state capacity, infrastructure, international demand, and the timing of reform shaped its opportunities. A country adopting parts of the model must assess which of those conditions it shares and which it would need to build.

prefix: The decision to build Jebel Ali Port
old_text: The decision to build Jebel Ali Port in the late 1970s seemed even more irrational. Dubai was already building the region's largest port at Port Rashid, yet Sheikh Rashid ordered construction of an even larger port 35 kilometers away. Jebel Ali would be the world's largest man-made harbor, capable of handling the world's largest ships, in a region that barely registered in global trade. A Government of Dubai announcement in August 1976 estimated the 74-berth harbor's cost at AED3 billion. Government of Dubai, 2 August 1976. International advisors universally recommended against it. Sheikh Rashid's response was characteristic: "Build it bigger."
new_text: The decision to build Jebel Ali Port in the late 1970s extended Dubai's investment in maritime capacity. A Government of Dubai announcement in August 1976 estimated the 74-berth harbor's cost at AED3 billion. The investment posed the central question for infrastructure-led development: would the services attract enough new activity to justify capacity built ahead of demand? Government of Dubai, 2 August 1976.

old_text: The Middle East in the 1980s was not business-friendly by any definition. Most countries required local partners for foreign companies, meaning 51% ownership by nationals who often contributed nothing but their passport. Corporate taxes ranged from 35% to 55%. Import duties could exceed 100%. Currency controls prevented profit repatriation. Bureaucracy was legendary—company registration could take months, licenses years, permits forever. Corruption was endemic though never acknowledged. The idea that a Middle Eastern country would offer 100% foreign ownership, zero taxes, and efficient administration seemed impossible.
new_text: JAFZA's offer addressed ownership, taxation, customs, and administrative costs that foreign businesses had to evaluate when entering the region. These requirements differed by country and activity. A zone could distinguish itself by making the applicable terms clear and providing the services needed to operate under them.

old_text: Dubai Media City, launched simultaneously, targeted a different challenge: making Dubai the media capital of a region where media was heavily controlled. Every Middle Eastern country censored media, restricted foreign ownership, and controlled content. Dubai Media City offered something unprecedented: a free media zone where international standards applied. CNN, BBC, Reuters, and Bloomberg established regional operations, broadcasting from Dubai to the entire region.
new_text: Dubai Media City brought broadcasters, news organizations, and related services into a specialized location. Its appeal depended on facilities, regional access, and the permissions available to media businesses. A specialized zone's operating terms need to be assessed under its actual law; the presence of international firms does not establish unrestricted freedom of activity.

prefix: Consistent leadership and commitment were perhaps
old_text: Consistent leadership and commitment were perhaps the most important factors. The ruling families of Dubai and Abu Dhabi maintained consistent development strategies across generations. This wasn't democratic in the Western sense, but it was remarkably responsive to economic needs. Decisions that would take years in democratic countries took days in the UAE. Infrastructure that would face endless environmental reviews and community objections elsewhere was built immediately. This speed was competitive advantage.
new_text: Continuity of development policy helped Dubai and Abu Dhabi sustain investments across generations of leadership. Concentrated authority can speed decisions, but speed alone does not establish their quality. A zone must also provide environmental review, community participation, and a way to challenge decisions that affect people's rights.

old_text: Environmental sustainability challenges everything about the UAE model. The country has among the world's highest per capita carbon footprints. Dubai's ecological footprint is ten times what the land can support. Water comes entirely from energy-intensive desalination. Air conditioning runs continuously in the desert heat. The indoor ski slope in Mall of the Emirates epitomizes the absurdity—snow in the desert maintained through massive energy consumption. Climate change, which the UAE's development exacerbates, threatens the country's existence through sea-level rise and extreme heat.
new_text: The UAE's development raises substantial questions about energy and water use. Desalination supplies much of its potable water, alongside groundwater and other sources used for different purposes. Cooling, transport, construction, and water production all need to be included in an assessment of a zone's resource demands. The design question is how to provide those services reliably while reducing emissions and environmental damage. UAE Government, water resources overview.

old_text: Social cohesion challenges grow as the contradictions of the UAE model become apparent. Emiratis, who comprise less than 10% of the population, live separately from expatriates. The social contract—economic opportunity in exchange for political silence—works for skilled expatriates but creates resentment among both locals (who feel marginalized) and workers (who feel exploited). [ad]The lack of integration means that despite decades of residence, expatriates have no path to citizenship and no real belonging.
new_text: An economy that relies on expatriate labor must also address residence, family life, participation, and long-term security. UAE citizenship is available to specified categories under conditions, including reforms announced in January 2021 for investors, professionals, and people with particular talents. Those routes do not by themselves answer how a zone includes its wider workforce or how residents can challenge unfair treatment. Dubai Media Office, 30 January 2021.

prefix: Jurisdictional portability also solves Africa's credibility
old_text: Jurisdictional portability also solves Africa's credibility problem. A Nigerian company that operates successfully in Lagos generates no credibility internationally because Nigeria's institutional weakness taints all Nigerian businesses. But a Nigerian company operating through the network protocol—with its compliance history, governance structure, and operational track record recorded immutably and verified continuously—can demonstrate credibility regardless of geographic origin. The asset's track record transcends its jurisdictional home.
new_text: A company may have difficulty demonstrating its record abroad when receiving institutions cannot readily verify its domestic evidence. A recognition agreement could help a Nigerian business present specified records to an authorized counterparty elsewhere. The counterparty would still assess the evidence, the business, and the risks relevant to the proposed activity. Portability can reduce an information problem; it does not remove commercial or country risk.

old_text: Mauritius stands alone as Africa's unambiguous SEZ success story, transforming from a sugar monoculture to an upper-middle-income diversified economy. Understanding why Mauritius succeeded where others failed provides crucial lessons for zone development across Africa and beyond.
new_text: Mauritius provides a widely studied African example of export-oriented industrial development. Its transition from dependence on sugar toward a more diversified economy raises questions about market access, investment, administrative capacity, and the way zone benefits can reach firms outside a physical enclave.

old_text: Yet Mauritius had advantages that weren't immediately apparent. The island had avoided the worst of colonialism's extractive institutions. There were no mines to create enclave economies. No white settler population claimed the best land. No traditional kingdoms were destroyed to create the colony. The sugar plantation economy, while exploitative, had created infrastructure (ports, roads, communications) and institutions (banks, trading houses, legal systems) that could be repurposed for development.
new_text: Mauritius had institutions and infrastructure that could support a change in economic activity, including ports, trading relationships, banks, and a legal system. Those inherited resources did not remove the harms of colonialism or the inequality of the plantation economy. The development question was how to adapt them to a broader range of businesses and employment.

prefix: Employment and exports grew with the number
old_text: Employment and exports grew with the number of enterprises. EPZ employment grew from zero in 1970 to 90,000 by 1990, mostly women entering the workforce for the first time. EPZ exports increased from nothing to over $2 billion, surpassing sugar as the main foreign exchange earner. The number of EPZ enterprises reached 500, mostly locally owned as Mauritians learned from foreign partners. Unemployment fell from 20% to effectively zero, creating labor shortages that drove wage increases.

prefix: The Calabar Free Trade Zone, established
old_text: The Calabar Free Trade Zone, established in 1992, exemplifies Nigeria's challenges. Located in Cross River State near the Cameroon border, Calabar seemed ideally positioned to serve West and Central African markets. The state government allocated 260 hectares, promised infrastructure, and offered generous incentives. International partners, including Malaysian investors, expressed interest. Yet thirty years later, the zone operates at less than 20% capacity, with most plots undeveloped and few manufacturers operating successfully.
new_text: A 2011 World Bank study contrasted Calabar's manufacturing ambition with a zone serving the oil and gas sector near Port Harcourt. It reported limited manufacturing activity at Calabar despite substantial investment, while the sector-focused initiative had attracted considerably more employment. The comparison concerns that study's period; it shows why a zone's fit with existing economic activity matters. Farole, World Bank, 2011, box 3.2, p. 78.

old_text: Infrastructure repeatedly falls short of the zone's promises. The zone's marketing materials promise reliable electricity, but manufacturers report outages lasting days. The "24-hour water supply" comes from boreholes that run dry in dry seasons. The "modern telecommunications" consists of unreliable mobile networks. The "direct port access" requires navigating 100 kilometers of roads that become impassable during rains. Companies spend more on infrastructure than production, defeating the purpose of zone incentives.
new_text: For manufacturers, unreliable power, water, roads, or port access can erase the value of an incentive. The operator needs to specify the service promised, the party responsible, the standard measured, and the remedy when it fails. Marketing material alone cannot establish that a facility delivers those services.

old_text: The infrastructure problems reflect deeper failures in governance. Operating in Calabar requires dealing with federal, state, and local authorities, each claiming jurisdiction and demanding payments. The Nigerian Export Processing Zone Authority (NEPZA) supposedly provides one-stop services, but has no power over customs (federal), immigration (federal), environmental protection (federal and state), labor inspection (state), or land allocation (state and local). Companies report dealing with over 30 agencies, each with its own requirements, fees, and informal expectations.
new_text: Administrative coordination matters for the same reason. A one-stop office can help an investor navigate requirements, but its usefulness depends on the powers and cooperation of the authorities behind it. Customs, immigration, environmental review, employment, and land rights need defined responsibilities and working procedures.

prefix: The corruption tax makes formal taxes irrelevant
old_text: The corruption tax makes formal taxes irrelevant. Every interaction requires facilitation payments: to clear customs (despite duty-free status), to get work permits (despite zone privileges), to connect utilities (despite official tariffs), to move goods (despite free movement rights). These payments aren't fixed or predictable but negotiated each time, creating uncertainty that no business plan can accommodate. A zone manager admitted privately that the informal costs exceed the formal savings, making the zone more expensive than operating outside it.
new_text: Unofficial payments, where they occur, add cost and uncertainty beyond published fees. A credible zone should make its charges and decision procedures visible, record requests and outcomes, and provide a route for complaints. Evaluating those arrangements requires evidence from actual operations.

prefix: Security adds another layer of cost
old_text: Security adds another layer of cost and complexity. The Calabar zone has experienced kidnappings of foreign managers, theft of equipment, and vandalism of facilities. Companies hire private security that costs more than their local workforce. The federal police provide little protection unless separately compensated. The community relations require constant negotiation, with local leaders demanding employment quotas, contracts, and contributions. One manufacturer relocated to Ghana after his third kidnapping, despite having invested millions in facilities.
new_text: Security and community relations also belong in the operating plan. Businesses need protection for people and assets, and communities need a voice in decisions about land, employment, and services. The responsible institutions and the cost of their work should be explicit before investment begins.

old_text: The Dangote Refinery, located within the Lekki zone, shows both the potential and the pathology of Nigerian development. This $20 billion project, Africa's largest oil refinery, demonstrates that massive industrial projects are possible in Nigeria. But it also reveals the dysfunction: the project took twice as long as planned, cost twice the budget, and required Aliko Dangote's personal intervention with successive presidents to overcome regulatory obstacles. The obstacles faced by Africa's richest man indicate the difficulty ordinary investors face.
new_text: The refinery in Lekki's southeast quadrant also illustrates why the development cannot be judged as a single concession. A large industrial project has its own financing, infrastructure, approvals, and operating record. Its performance should be assessed separately from neighboring zones and from the wider masterplan.

old_text: The Nigerian paradox deepens when considering the entrepreneurial energy that thrives despite the dysfunction. Lagos has become Africa's startup capital, with companies like Flutterwave, Paystack, and Andela achieving unicorn valuations. Nollywood produces more films than Hollywood. Nigerian musicians dominate global Afrobeats.[ah] The creative and digital economies flourish while the physical economy stagnates. This suggests that physical infrastructure and governance systems lag Nigeria's human capabilities.
new_text: The contrast between digital businesses and infrastructure-intensive production poses a useful question: which constraints does a particular activity actually face? Software, professional services, manufacturing, and logistics need different combinations of skills, finance, utilities, and administration. Zone design should follow those needs rather than assume one national verdict covers them all.

old_text: Ethiopia's aggressive SEZ development from 2010 to 2020 represents the most ambitious attempt to replicate China's model in Africa. The government, inspired by China's success and advised by Chinese experts, believed that authoritarian efficiency could overcome Africa's development challenges. The failure of this model provides crucial lessons about the limits of state-led development and the importance of political stability.
new_text: Ethiopia's industrial-park program sought to attract export manufacturing through dedicated facilities and coordinated public investment. Its experience raises separate questions about factory conditions, wages, productivity, infrastructure outside the parks, and political continuity. Those questions need separate evidence; the model cannot be assessed from construction speed alone.

old_text: But the success was superficial, masking deep problems that would soon emerge. A May 2019 NYU Stern study reported entry-level base pay of about US$26 per month at Hawassa. It described Ethiopia's garment-sector base wage as the lowest among garment-producing countries; incentives could supplement that base pay. NYU Stern, May 2019, pp. 1, 4, 9 and 12. This wasn't enough to live on even by Ethiopian standards. Workers slept eight to a room in slums outside the park. They couldn't afford transportation, walking hours to work. They couldn't afford food, surviving on bread and tea. Turnover exceeded 100% annually, meaning the entire workforce quit and was replaced every year.

old_text: The political implosion from 2018 exposed the fundamental fragility of authoritarian development. When Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed took power and loosened political controls, long-suppressed ethnic tensions exploded. The Tigray War that began in 2020 devastated the country, including the industrial zones. Hawassa shut down repeatedly due to ethnic violence. Foreign investors fled. International brands suspended sourcing. The industrial transformation reversed overnight.
new_text: Political conflict can disrupt the conditions on which a park depends: transport, power, staff movement, market access, and the willingness of customers to place orders. Ethiopia's conflict illustrates why an operating plan must address risks outside the park boundary. Records held elsewhere may help a company establish its standing after disruption, but cannot protect a factory or guarantee continued access to export markets.

old_text: The Ethiopian experience demonstrates that the Chinese model requires more than authoritarian government and cheap labor. It requires state capacity that most African countries lack, political stability that authoritarianism doesn't guarantee, and social cohesion that forced industrialization can destroy. Ethiopia tried to compress into a decade what China achieved over forty years, without China's advantages of size, homogeneity, and timing. The result was catastrophic failure that set back Ethiopian development by decades.
new_text: The Ethiopian case makes political continuity, worker welfare, and connections to the surrounding economy central to the design question. Dedicated facilities cannot supply all of those conditions. A zone needs both an operating institution and a plan for dependencies it does not control.

old_text: Since 2006, China has established or participated in over 20 SEZs across Africa, representing a new model of zone development that differs from both traditional Western approaches and indigenous African efforts. These zones, part of China's Belt and Road Initiative, promise to bring Chinese efficiency, capital, and market access to African industrialization. The reality has been mixed, with some successes, many failures, and persistent questions about whether this represents partnership or exploitation.
new_text: Chinese-backed economic cooperation zones in Africa involve different developers, sectors, financing arrangements, and relationships with host governments. Their outcomes should be compared at that level. Appendix B distinguishes the Eastern Industrial Park, the Zambia–China zone, and Lekki's separately managed concessions.

old_text: But deeper examination reveals problems. The zone operates as a Chinese enclave with minimal integration into the Ethiopian economy. Chinese managers live in separate compounds. Chinese workers, imported despite Ethiopian unemployment, handle skilled tasks. Chinese suppliers provide inputs. Chinese buyers purchase outputs. Its operations remain weakly connected to Ethiopia's economy. Technology transfer, the great promise of Chinese investment, remains minimal. Ethiopian workers perform basic tasks without learning advanced skills.
new_text: Employment and investment totals leave further questions about local participation. Which skilled jobs do local workers hold? Which inputs come from domestic suppliers? What training occurs, and can workers use those skills elsewhere? These measures help distinguish an enclave from a development that strengthens the surrounding economy.

old_text: The environmental and social impacts raise further concerns. Chinese companies, escaping environmental regulations at home, sometimes treat Africa as a pollution haven. Waste disposal is inadequate. Worker safety standards are minimal. Community consultation is absent. When local communities protest, Chinese managers call Ethiopian security forces for suppression rather than engage in dialogue. The zones generate growth but also grievance.
new_text: Environmental and social performance require their own evidence. A zone should publish applicable waste and safety requirements, assign inspection responsibility, and provide procedures for community consultation and complaints. Neither foreign sponsorship nor rapid construction establishes that these obligations have been met.
